title: What does a cache hit save?
answer: A hit saves the database read; a miss still makes it, and adds a cache read and write

checks.question: Nine of ten requests for one user are hits. How many database reads do those ten requests make, against how many before the change?
checks.answer: One, the miss that filled the cache, against ten. Each hit returns from KV without reaching D1.

checks.question: A nightly job looks up every user exactly once. What does the cache do to its database reads, and to its total work?
checks.answer: Every lookup misses, so the job still makes one database read per user, as before, and each lookup adds a KV read and a KV write. The cache saves nothing here and costs two extra operations a user.

checks.question: For a user who does not exist, the query returns null. What happens on the next lookup for that user, and which line decides it?
checks.answer: It misses again and reads D1 again. The put stores the text null; get with "json" parses it back to null, and line 3, if (hit), treats null as no saved value. A missing user is never answered from the cache.

steps.title: Does this request need the database?
steps.line: Predict: a saved copy sits in front of the database. What does a cache hit cost?
steps.caption: The handler’s lookup function, getUser, answers each request with one database query, even when the same user was fetched a second ago. The change in this merge request puts a store of saved values, a cache, in front of that query. If the user’s value is already saved, the request is a hit; if not, a miss. Count the database reads for the selected request before and after the change.

steps.title: Answer: the hit skips the database
steps.line: The key already has a stored value.
steps.caption: A hit saves the database read; a miss still makes it, and adds a cache read and write. KV, the cache, already holds this user, so the request returns the saved value with zero database reads. Switch to the miss to see what the saving costs when the value is not there.
steps.picture: Request. KV hit. Response. Database reads: 0. Saved value returned.

steps.title: Answer: the miss still reads the database
steps.line: The key has no stored value yet.
steps.caption: A hit saves the database read; a miss still makes it, and adds a cache read and write. KV, the cache, has no entry for this user, so the request reads the database once, as before, stores the result in KV and returns it. A later request can use the saved value; this one did more work than it would have without the cache.

steps.line: After the empty lookup, lines 4 to 6 read D1, write KV and return.
steps.caption: Walked through the edited diagram and code, the miss finds nothing at line 3 and runs on: line 4 reads D1 as before the change, line 5 writes the row to KV for 300 seconds, and line 6 returns it. A later lookup for the same user can take the hit row until that entry expires, although KV can take 60 seconds or longer to show a new write in other locations.
